title: Streaming Fundamentals
summary: Unbounded data breaks the assumptions batch processing relies on. Learn the vocabulary — event time, delivery guarantees, throughput vs latency — that every other topic in this group builds on.

slides.markdown:
A batch job has a start, an end, and a known input size. A **stream** has none of those — it's a sequence of events that keeps arriving, with no promised final record.

That one difference forces a different mental model everywhere: you can't sort the whole dataset because there is no "whole," you can't wait for "all the data" before aggregating, and you have to decide what "done" even means for a window of time.

This topic is the vocabulary the rest of the group leans on — bounded vs unbounded, the three notions of time, delivery guarantees, and the throughput/latency trade-off. Get these solid and Kafka, watermarks, and exactly-once semantics all read as consequences of them, not new ideas.

slides.subTitle: Batch has an ending; a stream doesn't
slides.markdown:
**Bounded (batch) data** has a known size before you start: yesterday's log file, a full table export, a completed dataset. You can scan it twice, sort all of it, and define "finished" as "reached the last record."

**Unbounded (streaming) data** has no last record by definition — clicks, sensor readings, order events keep arriving as long as the system is live. Any answer you compute ("total revenue today") is a snapshot of a number that keeps changing.

This reframes the core question. Batch asks *"what's the answer over this fixed dataset?"* Streaming asks *"what's the answer so far, and when do I consider a window closed enough to emit?"* Every streaming-specific idea in this group — windowing, watermarks, state — exists to answer that second question.

slides.sectionTitle: Event time, processing time, ingestion time
slides.subTitle: Three clocks, three different answers
slides.markdown:
Every event carries (at least) three timestamps, and they can differ by seconds, minutes, or hours:

- **Event time** — when the event actually happened at the source (a tap on a phone, a sensor reading). This is usually what the business question wants.
- **Ingestion time** — when the event entered the streaming system (hit the message broker).
- **Processing time** — when a particular processing job actually handles it. This is whatever the wall clock reads when your code runs.

A mobile app can buffer events offline for hours before syncing. Its event time is 2pm; ingestion and processing time might both be 6pm. If you window "purchases per hour" using processing time, that 2pm purchase lands in the 6pm bucket — wrong answer, silently.

Default to event time for anything business-meaningful. Processing time is fine only for purely operational metrics like "events processed per second right now."

slides.subTitle: Time gaps at every hop
slides.markdown:
Trace one event from creation to result, and time gaps open up at every hop: it's produced on a device, waits in a local buffer, travels the network, sits in a broker's partition, gets picked up by a consumer, and finally lands in an aggregation.

Each hop adds delay that is invisible to the event itself — the event's *content* never says how long it waited. That's precisely why systems need a separate mechanism (watermarks, covered in the next topic) to estimate how much event-time data might still be in flight before declaring a window "done."

slides.markdown:
Three terms get thrown around loosely in interviews. Precisely:

- **At-most-once** — an event is delivered zero or one times. Fast and simple, but data can silently vanish on a failure. Fine for metrics you can afford to lose a few of.
- **At-least-once** — an event is delivered one or more times; the sender retries until it gets an acknowledgment. Nothing is lost, but retries can create duplicates.
- **Exactly-once** — the *effect* of processing happens exactly once, even though the underlying delivery may retry. This is a stronger, more expensive guarantee than either of the above and is usually built by combining at-least-once delivery with deduplication or idempotency (its own topic later in this group).

The interview trap: "exactly-once" describes a system's *end-to-end effect*, not a property any single network call can honestly promise on its own — a packet can always be lost or duplicated in transit.

slides.subTitle: The core streaming trade-off
slides.markdown:
**Throughput** is events processed per second. **Latency** is how long one event takes to go from arrival to result. They pull against each other:

| Lever | Higher throughput | Lower latency |
|---|---|---|
| Batching events before processing | larger batches | smaller batches (or none) |
| Network round trips | fewer, bulk calls | more, immediate calls |
| Buffering / windowing | wait to accumulate | emit as soon as possible |

A system that buffers 10,000 events before flushing amortizes per-call overhead across all of them — great throughput, but the first event in that batch waits for the other 9,999 before it's processed. Shrink the batch to 1 and latency drops close to network-plus-compute time, but per-event overhead now dominates and throughput falls.

Most real systems expose this as a tunable (batch size, linger time) rather than picking one side — you set it based on your actual SLA, not by maximizing either number in isolation.

It's tempting to assume events arrive in the order they were produced. They usually don't.

Network paths differ in latency, retries reorder delivery, and most brokers only guarantee order *within a partition*, not across an entire topic. Two events produced 10ms apart on different partitions can be processed in either order, or with a large gap.

Code that does `if event.timestamp < lastSeenTimestamp: discard` silently drops legitimately out-of-order data instead of handling it. The correct move is almost always to key events so related ones land on the same partition (preserving order where it matters) and to design aggregation logic that tolerates out-of-order arrival rather than assuming it away.

slides.subTitle: There's always a latency budget
slides.markdown:
Streaming systems still have latency — often milliseconds to a few seconds, sometimes more. The difference from batch isn't zero delay; it's that the delay is small and continuous instead of large and periodic.

Every streaming system design should state a **latency budget**: the maximum acceptable time from event occurrence to result being usable. A fraud-detection pipeline might need under 200ms end-to-end. A "trending topics" dashboard might tolerate 30 seconds. A near-real-time data warehouse sync might accept 5 minutes and still reasonably be called "streaming."

That budget, not the word "streaming" itself, should drive every downstream choice — which engine, how much buffering, whether you can afford exactly-once's overhead. Naming the budget up front is what separates a design that actually meets its SLA from one that just sounds fast.

slides.subTitle: Source, processing, sink, state
slides.markdown:
Every streaming pipeline, regardless of engine, decomposes into the same four pieces:

- **Source** — where events enter (a message broker topic, a change-data-capture feed, a socket).
- **Processing** — the transformations, filters, joins, and aggregations applied to each event or window of events.
- **Sink** — where results land (a database, another topic, a dashboard, an alert).
- **State** — anything processing needs to remember across events (a running count, the last-seen value for a key, a join buffer). State is what makes aggregation and joins possible on data that never fully arrives.

When you're handed an unfamiliar streaming architecture diagram, naming these four pieces first turns an intimidating box-and-arrow diagram into a checklist: what's the source's guarantee, what state does this stage hold, and what happens to that state on a crash?

Rough production scale to anchor the vocabulary: a mid-size e-commerce clickstream might push **20,000–50,000 events/second** at peak, each a few hundred bytes. A single well-tuned consumer instance can often keep up with several thousand events/second, so a pipeline at that scale needs dozens of parallel consumers — which is exactly why partitioning (splitting the stream so consumers can work independently) shows up in nearly every real design.

Latency budgets vary just as widely: a payment-fraud check might need a **p99 under 100ms**, while a "daily active users" streaming rollup might have a **multi-minute** budget and can afford heavier windowing and larger batches.

The lesson: "streaming" spans several orders of magnitude of both throughput and latency requirement. Knowing your actual numbers — events/second and the acceptable end-to-end delay — should come before picking an engine or a windowing strategy, not after.

With this vocabulary in place, the rest of the group builds on it directly:

- **Event time and watermarks** — how a system decides a window is "done" despite out-of-order arrival.
- **Windowing strategies** — the concrete shapes (tumbling, sliding, session) you group unbounded events into.
- **Stateful processing and exactly-once** — how state survives crashes, and what guarantee you can actually claim end-to-end.
- **Kafka and engine comparisons** — the concrete systems that implement all of the above, with real trade-offs between them.

Every one of those topics is really this topic's ideas made specific: a watermark is event time made actionable, a window is unbounded data made finite, and exactly-once is a delivery guarantee made precise enough to implement.
